--- title: "Principal Component Analysis" format: revealjs: logo: /images/lmjl.jpg footer: Data Science with R include-in-header: - text: | width: 1280 height: 700 margin: 0.03 center: false auto-animate-duration: 0.9 slide-number: true number-sections: false code-overflow: wrap include-after-body: - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/spread-script.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/mono-whitespace.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/logo-link.html - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/paper-adv-popup.html theme: [default, ../../../resources/slidecrafting/styles_template.scss, ../../../theme/scss/ensai-theme.scss] revealjs-plugins: - codewindow - tabset filters: - arrows - roughnotation - zoom-vp - ../../../resources/slidecrafting/code-pop.lua knitr: opts_chunk: dev.args: { bg: "transparent" } --- # Overview ## Dimensionality reduction {.build} **Problem.** Many variables make data hard to read and models risky (multicollinearity, overfitting, broken assumptions). **Question.** "How do I keep most of the information with only a few variables?"
$\Longrightarrow$ Reduce the dimension of the feature space.
Fewer relationships to juggle, and a much smaller risk of overfitting. ## PCA {.build} **What?** A *feature-extraction* technique: it **combines** the input variables so you can drop the least important ones while keeping the most valuable parts of all. A bonus: the new variables are mutually **independent**. **How?** It finds the directions, the **principal components**, in which the data vary most, assuming direction with the largest variance is the most *important*. **When?** You cannot hand-pick variables to drop; you want independent inputs; you can live with less interpretable variables. ## Principle ![](pca-principle.gif) - PC1 accounts for the largest possible variance: the direction where projections (red dots) spread out most. - PC2 is uncorrelated with PC1 and maximizes the *remaining* variance. - And so on. ## Mathematical formalism
**Context.** $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n$ a sample of $n$ *i.i.d.* random vectors in $\mathbb{R}^p$; $\mathbb{X}$ the $n \times p$ data matrix; $\Sigma$ the covariance of the $\mathbf{X}_i$'s. **1st PC.** Search a linear projection $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^p$ of maximal variance: $\mathbb{X}\mathbf{a}$, with per-coordinate variance $\mathrm{Var}([\mathbb{X}\mathbf{a}]_i) = \mathbf{a}^\top \Sigma \mathbf{a}$.
> - A constraint is needed, as the maximum does not exist over all of $\mathbb{R}^p$: impose $\| \mathbf{a} \| = 1$. > - Use the sample covariance $S$ (unbiased for $\Sigma$) and solve $\max_{\| \mathbf{a} \| = 1} \mathbf{a}^\top S \mathbf{a}$. > - Solution: an eigenvector of $S$ for the largest eigenvalue; the Lagrangian gives $S\mathbf{a} = \lambda \mathbf{a}$.
## R Packages {.build} ### Principal component computation - `prcomp()` / `princomp()` from base **stats**; - `PCA()` from [**FactoMineR**](https://factominer.free.fr); - `dudi.pca()` from [**ade4**](https://pbil.univ-lyon1.fr/ade4/home.php?lang=eng). ### Recommendation Use `FactoMineR::PCA()`. ### Extraction and visualization The **factoextra** package. ## Case Study **Decathlon data.** Athletes' performance during two events (Decastar, OlympicG); $41$ athletes described by $13$ variables. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Objectives {.build} Run a PCA on all athletes to: - **Study individuals.** Are some athletes close (similar results)? Establish *profiles*, oppose one group to another. - **Study variables.** Summarize the correlation matrix and look for *synthetic* variables; can one number summarize an athlete's performance? - **Link both.** Characterize each group of athletes by variables. ## PCA Terminology
::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](pca-decathlon.png){width=90%} ::: :::
**Individuals.** *Active* ones build the PCA; *supplementary* ones get coordinates predicted from it. **Variables.** *Active* ones build the PCA; *supplementary* ones are predicted too, either - *Continuous* (cols 11, 12): rank and points; - *Qualitative* (col 13): the meeting (Olympic Game / Decastar), used to color individuals by group.
## Data standardization {.build} ### Why it matters PCA maximizes *variance*, so units bias it: a variable in centimeters swamps one in meters, whatever their intrinsic variability.
$\Longrightarrow$ We need to scale the variables prior to PCA!
### A common solution: standardization $$ x_{ij} \leftarrow \frac{x_{ij} - \overline{x}_j}{\sqrt{\frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{\ell=1}^n (x_{\ell j} - \overline{x}_j)^2}} $$
$\Longrightarrow$ `PCA()` in [**FactoMineR**](http://factominer.free.fr) standardizes automatically.
## `PCA()` Syntax ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} PCA( # a data frame with n rows (individuals) and p columns (numeric variables) X = , # number of dimensions kept in the results (by default 5) ncp = , # a vector indicating the indexes of the supplementary individuals ind.sup = , # a vector indicating the indexes of the quantitative supplementary variables quanti.sup = , # a vector indicating the indexes of the categorical supplementary variables quali.sup = , # boolean, if TRUE (default) a graph is displayed graph = ) ``` ::: ## Running `PCA()` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} PCA(X = decathlon[, 1:10], graph = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` **Results for the Principal Component Analysis (PCA)** The analysis was performed on 41 individuals, described by 10 variables *The results are available in the following objects: name description 1 "$eig" "eigenvalues" 2 "$var" "results for the variables" 3 "$var$coord" "coord. for the variables" 4 "$var$cor" "correlations variables - dimensions" 5 "$var$cos2" "cos2 for the variables" 6 "$var$contrib" "contributions of the variables" 7 "$ind" "results for the individuals" 8 "$ind$coord" "coord. for the individuals" 9 "$ind$cos2" "cos2 for the individuals" 10 "$ind$contrib" "contributions of the individuals" 11 "$call" "summary statistics" 12 "$call$centre" "mean of the variables" 13 "$call$ecart.type" "standard error of the variables" 14 "$call$row.w" "weights for the individuals" 15 "$call$col.w" "weights for the variables" ``` ::: ::: ## Visualization and Interpretation {.build} ### The **factoextra** package Whatever engine you used (`prcomp()`, `PCA()`, `dudi.pca()`, `epPCA()`), **factoextra** extracts and visualizes the results uniformly. ### Useful functions - `get_eigenvalue()`: eigenvalues / variances of the components; - `fviz_screeplot()`: eigenvalues & proportion of explained variance; - `get_pca_ind()` / `get_pca_var()`: results for individuals / variables; - `fviz_pca_ind()` / `fviz_pca_var()`: plots for individuals / variables; - `fviz_pca_biplot()`: biplot of both. # Choice of the reduced dimension ## Eigenvalues / Variances
Eigenvalues measure the amount of variation retained by each principal component.
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} eig_val <- get_eigenvalue(res_pca) html_table(eig_val) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ## Choosing the appropriate number of PCs {.build} Eigenvalues drive how many PCs to keep.
**Guidelines.** - An eigenvalue $> 1$ means a PC accounts for more variance than a single standardized variable (a common cutoff when data are standardized); - Balance a small number of PCs (good reduction) against total explained variance; - Look for interesting patterns in the first few PCs.
**Graphical tool.** ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/screeplot-plot-1.png){width=90%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fviz_screeplot(res_pca, addlabels = TRUE) ``` :::
# Analysis of the variables ## Variable Information in PCA {.build} ### Variable information extraction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} var_info <- get_pca_var(res_pca) ``` ::: ### Components - `var_info$coord`: coordinates of the variables; - `var_info$cos2`: quality of representation, `var.cos2 = var.coord * var.coord`; - `var_info$contrib`: contribution to each PC, `(var.cos2 * 100) / (sum cos2 of the component)`. ### Usage - How well do the PCs *represent* each variable? - Describe each PC by its most contributing variables. ## `$coord`: Correlation variables & components ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
Property: column norms are 1 (eigenvectors). Consequence: each coordinate lies in $[-1,1]$.
# Contribution of PCs to variables ## `fviz_pca_var()`: Correlation circle ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fviz_pca_var(res_pca, col.var = "black") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-corrcirc-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## `$cos2`: Quality of representation ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
**Positive** or **negative** strong correlations of a PC to a variable mean the PC represents it well. **Squared** correlations therefore measure representation quality.
## `$cos2`: Graphical tool 1 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot::corrplot(var_info$cos2, is.corr = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-cos2-plot1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## `$cos2`: Graphical tool 2 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Total cos2 of variables on Dim.1 and Dim.2 factoextra::fviz_cos2(res_pca, choice = "var", axes = 1:2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-cos2-plot2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## `$cos2`: Summary {.build}
- High `cos2` means the variable is well represented by that PC; - Low `cos2` means it is poorly represented; - Near the circle: **very well** represented by the first two PCs; - Near the center: **not well** represented.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-plot-res-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: :::
::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fviz_pca_var(X = res_pca, col.var = "cos2", gradient.cols = viridis(3), repel = TRUE) ``` :::
# Contribution of variables to PCs ## `$contrib`: Important variables ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
- Most important: variables correlating with `Dim.1` and `Dim.2`; - Variables correlating with no PC (or only the last ones) can be removed.
## `$contrib`: Graphical tool 1 ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot::corrplot(var_info$contrib, is.corr = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-contrib-plot1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## `$contrib`: Graphical tool 2
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Contributions of variables to PC1 factoextra::fviz_contrib( X = res_pca, choice = "var", axes = 1, top = 10 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-contrib-plot2-pc1-1.png){fig-align='center' width=99%} ::: :::
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Contributions of variables to PC2 factoextra::fviz_contrib( X = res_pca, choice = "var", axes = 2, top = 10 ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-contrib-plot2-pc2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=99%} ::: :::
## `$contrib`: Summary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} factoextra::fviz_pca_var( X = res_pca, col.var = "contrib", gradient.cols = viridis::viridis(3), repel = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/pca-var-contrib-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Component description ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_pca_var_desc <- FactoMineR::dimdesc(res = res_pca, axes = c(1, 2), proba = 0.05) ``` :::
**Description of PC1** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
**Description of PC2** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: :::
# Analysis of the individuals ## The reduced space ### Individual information extraction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ind_info <- get_pca_ind(res_pca) ``` ::: ### Components - `ind_info$coord`: coordinates of the individuals; - `ind_info$cos2`: quality of representation, `ind.cos2 = ind.coord * ind.coord`; - `ind_info$contrib`: contribution of individuals, `(ind.cos2 * 100) / (sum cos2 of the component)`. ### Usage - The reduced space eases pattern spotting, if it represents them well; - Similar individuals are grouped together on the plot. ## First factorial plane & quality ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} factoextra::fviz_pca_ind( X = res_pca, col.ind = "cos2", gradient.cols = viridis::viridis(3), repel = TRUE # Avoid text overlapping (slow if many points) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/res-pca-ind-cos2-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## First factorial plane & contribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Total contribution on PC1 and PC2 factoextra::fviz_contrib(res_pca, choice = "ind", axes = 1:2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/res-pca-ind-contrib-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## First factorial plane colored by groups ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} factoextra::fviz_pca_ind( X = res_pca, col.ind = decathlon$competition[1:23], # color by groups palette = viridis::viridis(3), addEllipses = TRUE, # Concentration ellipses legend.title = "Competition" ) ``` :::
- Shows whether a factorial plane *discriminates* individuals by a feature; - Here Olympics score positively on PC1, Decastar negatively; - But the ellipses overlap significantly.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/res-pca-competition-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=95%} ::: :::
# Combined variable and individual analysis ## Biplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fviz_pca_biplot(res_pca, repel = TRUE, col.var = "#2E9FDF", col.ind = "#696969") ``` :::
- Only useful with few variables & individuals, else unreadable; - Individuals and variables are not on the same scale: read *directions*, not absolute positions; - An individual on the same side as a variable has a high value for it; opposite side, a low value.
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](12-PCA-Slides_files/figure-revealjs/res-pca-biplot-plot-1.png){fig-align='center' width=95%} ::: :::
## Interpretation {.build} - The first two dimensions resume 50% of total inertia (total variance); - `100m` correlates negatively with `long.jump`: a short time goes with a big jump; - Axis 1 opposes athletes **good everywhere** (Karpov, Olympic) to those **bad everywhere** (Bourguignon, Decastar); - Axis 2 opposes **strong** (`Discus`, `Shot.put`) to **weak** athletes; - Strength is not much correlated with speed.
$\Longrightarrow$ Four profiles: fast+strong (Sebrle), slow (Casarsa), fast but weak (Warners), slow and weak (Lorenzo).
## Your turn - Download the lab file and related data sets from the course website in a folder on your computer. - Open the file `12-PCA-Exercises.qmd` and perform the PCA analyses for the proposed data sets. ## References - - - - -

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
